memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "When one of them dies and falls on something, that article, whatever its use, will be unclean, whether it is made of wood, cloth, hide or sackcloth. Put it in water; it will be unclean till evening, and then it will be clean." - Lev 11:32 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Now it is not people who are affected, but things. A dead lizard falls onto a wooden bowl, a cloth, a leather bag — and that object is unclean. Whatever its use, God says. No exceptions for the valuable item or the favourite one.

But look at how the verse ends. Put it in water. Unclean till evening. And then it will be clean.

That last phrase is the gift. God does not tell them to destroy the bowl. He gives a way back. Every single one of these regulations comes with a road to restoration — washing, waiting, and then clean again.

We can be far harsher with ourselves than God is. We assume that once something is spoiled it is finished. A relationship damaged, a testimony dented, a year wasted, a failure that feels permanent. We write it off as beyond repair.

But our God is a restorer. He speaks of restoring the years the locusts have eaten (Joel 2:25). He takes what is broken and does not discard it. In Christ we are not merely tolerated after failure — we are washed, and made new (Titus 3:5).

Whatever you think is past saving today, bring it to Him. And then it will be clean.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. What have you written off as beyond repair?
2. Do you believe God is a restorer, or only a judge?
3. What would it look like to bring that broken thing to God this week?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, thank You that You do not discard what is spoiled but wash and restore it. I bring You the things I have given up on, and I ask You to make them clean. Amen.
